inline.s: Therefore, practitioners should, in accordance with conditions, let their old karma dissolve and refrain from creating new misfortunes.
Bhikkhus! A bhikkhu contemplates phenomena as phenomena, that is, he contemplates phenomena in terms of the five aggregates subject to clinging.
Bhikkhus! How does a bhikkhu contemplate phenomena as phenomena, that is, how does he contemplate phenomena in terms of the five aggregates subject to clinging?
Bhikkhus! A bhikkhu clearly knows:
‘This is form; this is the arising of form; this is the ceasing of form;
‘This is feeling; this is the arising of feeling; this is the ceasing of feeling;
‘This is perception; this is the arising of perception; this is the ceasing of perception;
‘These are mental formations; this is the arising of mental formations; this is the ceasing of mental formations;
‘This is consciousness; this is the arising of consciousness; this is the ceasing of consciousness.’
Bhikkhus! This is how a bhikkhu contemplates phenomena as phenomena, that is, he contemplates phenomena in terms of the five aggregates subject to clinging.

blocks.text: 3. Contemplating the Sense Faculties and Sense Objects

inline.s: Contemplating the six sense faculties and the six sense objects, in order to awaken to the source of bondage.

[The six sense faculties] are the six internal bases: the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. The eye is the faculty of seeing, the ear of hearing, the nose of smelling, the tongue of tasting, the body of touching, and the mind of thinking. A root means that from which things grow — just as a plant with roots puts forth branches and trunks, so consciousness arises dependent upon conditions, and with the six faculties the six consciousnesses arise, in the same way. [The six sense objects] are the six external bases: form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental objects. An object means that which defiles; it can defile the pure minds of people and prevent true nature from manifesting. They are also called the six realms, that is, the external objects to which the six faculties are directed. [The six consciousnesses] are eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness. These are the discriminating functions of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and thinking that arise when the six faculties meet the six objects of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental objects.
Bhikkhus! A bhikkhu contemplates phenomena as phenomena, that is, he contemplates phenomena in terms of the six internal bases and the six external bases.
Bhikkhus! How does a bhikkhu contemplate phenomena as phenomena, that is, how does he contemplate phenomena in terms of the six internal bases and the six external bases?

Bhikkhus! A bhikkhu clearly knows the eye faculty, clearly knows forms, and clearly knows the fetter that arises dependent upon these two. He clearly knows that the unarisen fetter has arisen; he clearly knows that the fetter that has arisen has been abandoned; he clearly knows that the fetter now abandoned will not arise again in the future.

A bhikkhu clearly knows the ear faculty, clearly knows sounds, and clearly knows the fetter that arises dependent upon these two. He clearly knows that the unarisen fetter has arisen; he clearly knows that the fetter that has arisen has been abandoned; he clearly knows that the fetter now abandoned will not arise again in the future.

A bhikkhu clearly knows the nose faculty, clearly knows smells, and clearly knows the fetter that arises dependent upon these two. He clearly knows that the unarisen fetter has arisen; he clearly knows that the fetter that has arisen has been abandoned; he clearly knows that the fetter now abandoned will not arise again in the future.

A bhikkhu clearly knows the tongue faculty, clearly knows tastes, and clearly knows the fetter that arises dependent upon these two. He clearly knows that the unarisen fetter has arisen; he clearly knows that the fetter that has arisen has been abandoned; he clearly knows that the fetter now abandoned will not arise again in the future.

A bhikkhu clearly knows the body faculty, clearly knows tangibles, and clearly knows the fetter that arises dependent upon these two. He clearly knows that the unarisen fetter has arisen; he clearly knows that the fetter that has arisen has been abandoned; he clearly knows that the fetter now abandoned will not arise again in the future.

A bhikkhu clearly knows the mind faculty, clearly knows mental objects, and clearly knows the fetter that arises dependent upon these two. He clearly knows that the unarisen fetter has arisen; he clearly knows that the fetter that has arisen has been abandoned; he clearly knows that the fetter now abandoned will not arise again in the future.
[The mind faculty] The seventh of the eight consciousnesses, the manas consciousness, is the mind faculty.

[The eight consciousnesses] ālayavijñāna, manas-vijñāna, mano-vijñāna, eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, and body-consciousness. Among these, the ālayavijñāna is the fundamental consciousness; the other seven consciousnesses are all derived from it. [The mental object] That which the mind faculty takes as its object (the karmic seeds) is called the mental object.
Bhikkhus! This is how a bhikkhu contemplates phenomena as phenomena, that is, he contemplates phenomena in terms of the six internal bases and the six external bases.

blocks.text: 4. Contemplating the Seven Factors of Enlightenment

inline.s: The Amitābha Buddha Sūtra says:

‘In that land there are always many kinds of wonderful and richly colored birds: white cranes, peacocks, parrots, śarīs, kalaviṅkas, and two-hearted birds. These many birds, through the six periods of day and night, sing forth harmonious and beautiful sounds. Their songs proclaim the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eight factors of the noble path, and teachings such as these.’
The Vimalakīrti Sūtra says:
‘The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are the bodhisattva’s Pure Land.’
From this we can see the importance of cultivating the seven factors of enlightenment.
the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment

the four establishments of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold path (that is, the eight factors of the noble path). [The four establishments of mindfulness] First, contemplation of the body; second, contemplation of feeling; third, contemplation of mind; fourth, contemplation of phenomena. [The four right efforts] ‘Right effort’ means the ability to practice with great diligence: abandon evil that has already arisen, prevent evil that has not yet arisen, give rise to good that has not yet arisen, and increase the good that has already arisen. Practicing these four aspects of the path with vigor, urging on body, speech, and mind, to cut off evil and cultivate good. [The four bases of psychic power] Also called the four roads to psychic power; by cultivating these four one can realize supernormal powers at will. First, the base of psychic power of desire — the increase of the aspiration to cultivate the path and attain its fruit; second, the base of psychic power of mind — single-minded thought, abiding in right principle; third, the base of psychic power of energy — vigorous advance with no break in the work; fourth, the base of psychic power of wisdom — true illumination free from delusion, the mind no longer distracted.

[The five faculties] The faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. These five are the roots from which the noble path is born, hence they are called the ‘five faculties.’ [The five powers] The strength produced when the five faculties are firmly established is called the ‘five powers’: faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. The power of faith is the growth of the faculty of faith, which destroys all wrong belief; the power of energy is the growth of the faculty of energy, which destroys the body’s sloth; the power of mindfulness is the growth of the faculty of mindfulness, which destroys all wrong thoughts; the power of concentration is the growth of the faculty of concentration, which destroys all scattered thinking; the power of wisdom is the growth of the faculty of wisdom, which destroys all the delusions of the three realms.
[Bodhi] Rendered into Chinese as ‘awakening,’ it is the great wisdom that cuts off afflictions. [The seven factors of enlightenment]

The seven kinds of awakening revealed through the five faculties and five powers. First, the factor of mindfulness — at all times reflecting on the true Dharma, keeping concentration and wisdom in balance; second, the factor of dharma-investigation — using wisdom to examine the true and the false of phenomena; third, the factor of energy — practicing the true Dharma with courageous vigor; fourth, the factor of joy — the mind, obtaining the good Dharma, gives rise to gladness; fifth, the factor of tranquillity — removing the gross afflictions of body and mind so as to attain ease and peace; sixth, the factor of concentration — the mind resting on a single object, no longer scattering; seventh, the factor of equanimity — letting go of all delusive phenomena and earnestly practicing the true Dharma.

[The eightfold path] The eightfold practice of the noble ones. First, right view, that is, correct understanding; second, right intention, that is, correct thinking; third, right speech, that is, proper speech; fourth, right action, that is, proper conduct; fifth, right livelihood, that is, a proper occupation or way of life; sixth, right effort, that is, proper striving; seventh, right mindfulness, that is, correct attention; eighth, right concentration, that is, correct concentration. By cultivating this eightfold path one can realize the fruit of arhatship.
And further, bhikkhus! How does a bhikkhu contemplate phenomena as phenomena?
Bhikkhus! A bhikkhu contemplates phenomena as phenomena, that is, he contemplates phenomena in terms of the seven factors of enlightenment.
Bhikkhus! How does a bhikkhu contemplate phenomena as phenomena, that is, how does he contemplate phenomena in terms of the seven factors of enlightenment?

Bhikkhus! When a bhikkhu has the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, he clearly knows: ‘I have the factor of mindfulness’; when a bhikkhu does not have the factor of mindfulness, he clearly knows: ‘I do not have the factor of mindfulness.’ He clearly knows that the unarisen factor of mindfulness has arisen; he clearly knows that the arisen factor of mindfulness has reached full development.

When a bhikkhu has the factor of enlightenment of dharma-investigation, he clearly knows: ‘I have the factor of dharma-investigation’; when a bhikkhu does not have the factor of dharma-investigation, he clearly knows: ‘I do not have the factor of dharma-investigation.’ He clearly knows that the unarisen factor of dharma-investigation has arisen; he clearly knows that the arisen factor of dharma-investigation has reached full development.

When a bhikkhu has the factor of enlightenment of energy, he clearly knows: ‘I have the factor of energy’; when a bhikkhu does not have the factor of energy, he clearly knows: ‘I do not have the factor of energy.’ He clearly knows that the unarisen factor of energy has arisen; he clearly knows that the arisen factor of energy has reached full development.

When a bhikkhu has the factor of enlightenment of joy, he clearly knows: ‘I have the factor of joy’; when a bhikkhu does not have the factor of joy, he clearly knows: ‘I do not have the factor of joy.’ He clearly knows that the unarisen factor of joy has arisen; he clearly knows that the arisen factor of joy has reached full development.

When a bhikkhu has the factor of enlightenment of tranquillity, he clearly knows: ‘I have the factor of tranquillity’; when a bhikkhu does not have the factor of tranquillity, he clearly knows: ‘I do not have the factor of tranquillity.’ He clearly knows that the unarisen factor of tranquillity has arisen; he clearly knows that the arisen factor of tranquillity has reached full development.

When a bhikkhu has the factor of enlightenment of concentration, he clearly knows: ‘I have the factor of concentration’; when a bhikkhu does not have the factor of concentration, he clearly knows: ‘I do not have the factor of concentration.’ He clearly knows that the unarisen factor of concentration has arisen; he clearly knows that the arisen factor of concentration has reached full development.

When a bhikkhu has the factor of enlightenment of equanimity, he clearly knows: ‘I have the factor of equanimity’; when a bhikkhu does not have the factor of equanimity, he clearly knows: ‘I do not have the factor of equanimity.’ He clearly knows that the unarisen factor of equanimity has arisen; he clearly knows that the arisen factor of equanimity has reached full development.

Then he clearly realizes: ‘This is the Dharma!’ Having cultivated a state of mere knowing and reflection, he transcends clinging and no longer craves or is averse to anything in body, mind, or the world.
Bhikkhus! This is how a bhikkhu contemplates phenomena as phenomena, that is, he contemplates phenomena in terms of the seven factors of enlightenment.
Craving is the root of the various sufferings, such as birth and death. The Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
‘All sentient beings, from time without beginning, because of manifold affections and craving, are caught up in the round of rebirth;
Know that the round of rebirth is rooted in love.
Therefore, sentient beings who wish to escape birth and death and free themselves from the round of rebirth should first cut off craving and remove the thirst of love.’
And the Four Noble Truths are the essential path that extinguishes craving and delivers one from all the suffering of birth and death.

The Four Noble Truths are: the truth of suffering, the truth of the origin of suffering, the truth of the cessation of suffering, and the truth of the path. The origin is the cause of suffering, and suffering is the result of the origin; the path is the cause of cessation, and cessation is the result of the path.

That is to say: the various sufferings of birth and death (suffering) are gathered together by craving (origin); and to extinguish craving (cessation), one can only cultivate the noble path (path). The Buddha said:
‘This is suffering, and you should understand it; this is the origin, and you should abandon it; this is the path, and you should cultivate it; this is cessation, and you should realize it.’
Therefore,
practitioners should be diligent and earnest, knowing suffering, abandoning its origin, cultivating the path, and realizing cessation

[Truth] The principle that is real and without error. [The Four Noble Truths] The truth of suffering, the truth of its origin, the truth of its cessation, and the truth of the path. First, the ‘truth of suffering’ sets forth the truth that life is filled with suffering. Suffering has the character of oppression. Life involves the three sufferings, the eight sufferings, and innumerable sufferings; suffering is the truth of actual human life. Second, ‘origin’ in the ‘truth of the origin of suffering’ means to gather and bring about; it sets forth the truth of how the suffering of life arises. The suffering of life is due to craving, and then to clinging, then to karma, then to suffering, then to rebirth. Third, the ‘truth of cessation’ sets forth the truth of extinguishing all suffering. When the whole origin of suffering (craving) is cut off forever without remainder, with no grasping and no clinging, one no longer creates karma, suffers, or is reborn; this is the truth of cessation. Fourth, the ‘truth of the path’ sets forth the truth of how forever to cut off the origin of suffering (craving), that is, the path to the extinction of suffering — the eightfold noble path. Among the Four Noble Truths, the origin is the cause and suffering is the result; the path is the cause and cessation is the result.

[The three sufferings] The suffering of suffering, the suffering of change, and the suffering of conditioned states. The suffering of suffering: worldly beings have a body subject to birth and death, which is already suffering enough, and with all kinds of suffering pressing upon them, it is suffering piled upon suffering, hence it is called the suffering of suffering; the suffering of change is the suffering felt when an occasional pleasant state is lost; the suffering of conditioned states is the suffering of all conditioned things being impermanent and ceaselessly flowing, never at rest. [The eight sufferings] First, the suffering of birth, the pain at the time of birth; second, the suffering of aging, the pain of old age and bodily weakness; third, the suffering of sickness, the pain of illness; fourth, the suffering of death, the pain at the time of death; fifth, the suffering of separation from the loved, the pain of parting with those one loves; sixth, the suffering of meeting with the hated, the pain of associating with those one hates; seventh, the suffering of not getting what one seeks, the pain of unfulfilled desires; eighth, the suffering of the raging of the five aggregates, the suffering in which the activity of the five aggregates (the five aggregates) blazes and covers over true nature. [The eightfold noble path] Also called the eightfold path, the eightfold practice of the noble ones: first, right view, correct understanding; second, right intention, correct thinking; third, right speech, proper speech; fourth, right action, proper conduct; fifth, right livelihood, a proper occupation and way of life; sixth, right effort, correct striving; seventh, right mindfulness, correct attention; eighth, right concentration, correct concentration. By cultivating this eightfold noble path one can realize the fruit of arhatship.
Bhikkhus! A bhikkhu contemplates phenomena as phenomena, that is, he contemplates phenomena in terms of the Four Noble Truths.
Bhikkhus! How does a bhikkhu contemplate phenomena as phenomena, that is, how does he contemplate phenomena in terms of the Four Noble Truths?

Bhikkhus! A bhikkhu clearly knows as it really is: this is suffering. He clearly knows as it really is: this is the origin of suffering. He clearly knows as it really is: this is the cessation of suffering. He clearly knows as it really is: this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.

And what, bhikkhus, is the noble truth of suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, death is suffering; sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are suffering; association with the hated is suffering; separation from the loved is suffering; not getting what one wants is suffering. In short, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering.

[The five aggregates subject to clinging] Clinging means grasping and clinging; an aggregate means accumulation; the aggregates arise from clinging, hence they are called aggregates subject to clinging. The five aggregates subject to clinging: first, the aggregate of form subject to clinging; second, the aggregate of feeling subject to clinging; third, the aggregate of perception subject to clinging; fourth, the aggregate of mental formations subject to clinging; fifth, the aggregate of consciousness subject to clinging.

And what, bhikkhus, is birth? For whatever beings, in whatever class of beings, there is the taking of rebirth, descent, arising, the emergence of the aggregates, and the obtaining of the internal and external bases — this, bhikkhus, is called birth.

And what, bhikkhus, is aging? For whatever beings, in whatever class of beings, there is the decay, decrepitude, the falling out of teeth, the greying of hair, the wrinkling of skin, the nearing of the end of life, and the exhaustion of the faculties — this, bhikkhus, is aging.

And what, bhikkhus, is death? For whatever beings, in whatever class of beings, there is the falling away, passing away, breaking up, disappearance, the ending of the life span, the dissolution of the aggregates, the abandoning of the body, and the cutting off of life — this, bhikkhus, is death.

And what, bhikkhus, is sorrow? Whenever anyone, at any time, affected by loss or misfortune, gives rise to these painful states of mind — sorrowing, mourning, grieving, deep grief, and profound lamentation — this, bhikkhus, is sorrow.

And what, bhikkhus, is lamentation? Whenever anyone, at any time, affected by loss or misfortune, gives rise to weeping, wailing, lamenting, and the state of wailing and lamenting — this, bhikkhus, is lamentation.
And what, bhikkhus, is pain? Bhikkhus! Whatever bodily pain, discomfort, or unpleasant feeling arises from bodily contact — this, bhikkhus, is pain.
And what, bhikkhus, is grief? Bhikkhus
— whatever mental pain, discomfort, or any painful, unpleasant feeling that arises from mental contact — this, bhikkhus, is grief.

And what, bhikkhus, is despair? Whenever anyone, at any time, affected by loss or misfortune, gives rise to these states of mind — agitation, distress, sorrowful agitation, and vexation — this, bhikkhus, is despair.

And what, bhikkhus, is the suffering of association with the hated? Whenever anyone, at any time or place, encounters unpleasant, disliked forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects, or at all times and places meets with misfortune, harm, hardship, or distress, and there is meeting, association, contact, or union with them — this, bhikkhus, is called the suffering of association with the hated.

And what, bhikkhus, is the suffering of separation from the loved? Whenever anyone, at any time or place, is separated from the agreeable, pleasing, beloved sense objects of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental objects; when people who wish him well and hope for his fortune, prosperity, comfort, or safety — such as parents, brothers and sisters, friends, colleagues, and relatives — are separated from him, so that he cannot see, approach, or associate with them — this, bhikkhus, is called the suffering of separation from the loved.

And what, bhikkhus, is the suffering of not getting what one wants? Bhikkhus! Beings who are subject to birth give rise to this wish: ‘May we not be subject to birth! May we not be reborn again!’ But this cannot be obtained by mere wishing — this is the suffering of not getting what one wants.
Bhikkhus! What is the suffering of not getting what one wants? Bhikkhus! Beings subject to aging give rise to this wish
‘May we not be subject to aging! May we not be subject to aging!’ But this cannot be obtained by mere wishing — this is the suffering of not getting what one wants.
Bhikkhus! What is the suffering of not getting what one wants? Bhikkhus! Beings subject to illness give rise to this wish
‘May we not be subject to illness! May we be free of illness!’ But this cannot be obtained by mere wishing — this is the suffering of not getting what one wants.
Bhikkhus! What is the suffering of not getting what one wants? Bhikkhus! Beings subject to death give rise to this wish
‘May we not be subject to death! May we never die!’ But this cannot be obtained by mere wishing — this is the suffering of not getting what one wants.
Bhikkhus! What is the suffering of not getting what one wants? Bhikkhus! Beings subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair give rise to this wish

‘May we not be subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair! May we no longer sorrow, lament, suffer pain, grieve, or despair!’ But this cannot be obtained by mere wishing — this is the suffering of not getting what one wants.

Bhikkhus! What is meant by ‘in short, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering’? The aggregate of form subject to clinging is suffering, the aggregate of feeling subject to clinging is suffering, the aggregate of perception subject to clinging is suffering, the aggregate of mental formations subject to clinging is suffering, the aggregate of consciousness subject to clinging is suffering. Bhikkhus! This is what is meant by ‘in short, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering.’
Bhikkhus! This is the noble truth of suffering.

Craving is the origin of suffering (craving brings about suffering) and is the root of suffering. Because of craving there is clinging; because of clinging, karma; because of karma, suffering; because of suffering, rebirth. Craving arises at the six faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind) meeting the six sense objects (form, sound, smell, taste, touch, mental object); therefore one must guard the gates of the six faculties, and upon contact with the sense objects, shine the light of awareness and cut off the root of delusion — this is the key.
And what, bhikkhus, is the noble truth of the origin of suffering?

It is craving, the craving that brings about continued rebirth, that is bound up with delight and lust, and that seeks delight here and there — that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence.

[Craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, craving for non-existence] Craving in the desire realm, craving in the form realm, and craving in the formless realm. [Craving in the formless realm] In the formless realm there is no materiality (dharmas of form), so there is also no body, palace, or physical object; there remains only the mind-consciousness, dwelling in deep and subtle concentration. Its craving is attachment to that deep, subtle concentration, delighting in its agreeableness and giving rise to clinging.
Bhikkhus! But where does this craving arise, and where does it establish itself?
In the world of body and mind, wherever there is something attractive and delightful, there craving arises and establishes itself.
And in the world of body and mind, what are the attractive and delightful things?
In the world of body and mind, the eye faculty is attractive and delightful, so craving arises there and establishes itself there;
In the world of body and mind, the ear faculty is attractive and delightful, so craving arises there and establishes itself there;
In the world of body and mind, the nose faculty is attractive and delightful, so craving arises there and establishes itself there;
In the world of body and mind, the tongue faculty is attractive and delightful, so craving arises there and establishes itself there;
In the world of body and mind, the body faculty is attractive and delightful, so craving arises there and establishes itself there;
In the world of body and mind, the mind faculty is attractive and delightful, so craving arises there and establishes itself there.
In the world of body and mind, the object of form is attractive and delightful, so craving arises there and establishes itself there;
In the world of body and mind, the object of sound is attractive and delightful, so craving arises there and establishes itself there;
In the world of body and mind, the object of smell is attractive and delightful, so craving arises there and establishes itself there;
In the world of body and mind, the object of taste is attractive and delightful, so craving arises there and establishes itself there;
In the world of body and mind, the object of touch is attractive and delightful, so craving arises there and establishes itself there;
In the world of body and mind, the mental object is attractive and delightful, so craving arises there and establishes itself there.
In the world of body and mind, eye-consciousness is attractive and delightful, so craving arises there and establishes itself there;
In the world of body and mind, ear-consciousness is attractive and delightful, so craving arises there and establishes itself there;
In the world of body and mind, nose-consciousness is attractive and delightful, so craving arises there and establishes itself there;
In the world of body and mind, tongue-consciousness is attractive and delightful, so craving arises there and establishes itself there;
In the world of body and mind, body-consciousness is attractive and delightful, so craving arises there and establishes itself there;
In the world of body and mind, mind-consciousness is attractive and delightful, so craving arises there and establishes itself there.
In the world of body and mind, eye-contact is attractive and delightful, so craving arises there and establishes itself there;
In the world of body and mind, ear-contact is attractive and delightful, so craving arises there and establishes itself there;
In the world of body and mind, nose-contact is attractive and delightful, so craving arises there and establishes itself there;
In the world of body and mind, tongue-contact is attractive and delightful, so craving arises there and establishes itself there;
In the world of body and mind, body-contact is attractive and delightful, so craving arises there and establishes itself there;
In the world of body and mind, mind-contact is attractive and delightful, so craving arises there and establishes itself there.
In the world of body and mind, feeling born of eye-contact is attractive and delightful, so craving arises there and establishes itself there;
In the world of body and mind, feeling born of ear-contact is attractive and delightful, so craving arises there and establishes itself there;
In the world of body and mind, feeling born of nose-contact is attractive and delightful, so craving arises there and establishes itself there;
In the world of body and mind, feeling born of tongue-contact is attractive and delightful, so craving arises there and establishes itself there;
In the world of body and mind, feeling born of body-contact is attractive and delightful, so craving arises there and establishes itself there;
In the world of body and mind, feeling born of mind-contact is attractive and delightful, so craving arises there and establishes itself there.
In the world of body and mind, perception arisen from the object of form is attractive and delightful, so craving arises there and establishes itself there;
In the world of body and mind, perception arisen from the object of sound is attractive and delightful, so craving arises there and establishes itself there;
In the world of body and mind, perception arisen from the object of smell is attractive and delightful, so craving arises there and establishes itself there;
